speechtext:
Has the government taken any steps to secure the repeal of the Imperial statute scheduling Canadian cattle imported into the United

Kingdom? Is it the intention of the government to press this very important question on the Imperial authorities at an early date?

In reply to the hon. gentleman, I may say that, as representing the government, I have taken every opportunity for a number of years back to urge this question upon the Imperial authorities, through Lord Stratheona chiefly. When I was in England myself 1 interviewed the Minister of Agriculture and the veterinary authorities of that department. I may say that I hope to proceed to England again this spring, and I shall make it my business to urge this matter with the utmost insistence upon the Imperial authorities, as I have continued to do ever since I have been in office.

speakeroldname: Mr. WM. H. BENNETT (East Simcoe) moved :
speechtext:
That in the opinion of this House, the time has arrived when a fixed and definite line of action should be undertaken on the question of the transportation of the grain and other commodities of the North-west Territories, Manitoba and the western states, with a view of centreing the same to the greatest possible extent in Canadian channels.
He said : Last year I had the honour of making a motion in the same terms as the one which I have just read. At that time it attracted the attention of a large number of gentlemen on either side of the House, and it also excited a considerable amount of attention and caused a large amount of discussion throughout the country by the public press, showing that the public are greatly interested in the question of transportation. The question of transportation is doubtless one of the largest questions in the public eye of Canada at the present time. That is shown by the fact that the Dominion government is from time to time expending large sums of money in the) improvement of the canal service and in the construction of railways, either directly or by granting large subsidies for that purpose. And beyond that, private capitalists are from time to time investing in railways In this country, or constructing railways,

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
showing, as it does, the great interest in the work. To the farmer of the western prairies the question of transportation is to-day probably the largest one before his view, because, the cheapening of grain transportation or carriage from the west to the east must result, in some part, in his participating in the cheapening of that transportation, and with the development of the northern part of Ontario, rich in mineral and timber resources, a great deal of interest centres in the fact that transportation may be cheapened from the west to the seaboard. The question also is of great importance in the province of Ontario and in other provinces in this that we are hoping to build up in the older provinces a large manufacturing trade and if we are to have customers for the manufactured products of these provinces we must after all expect to find them on our western prairies. The people of the older provinces, burdened as they have been for a great many years by raising large sums of money for the construction of railways in the west, and particularly the Canadian Pacific Railway, are anxious to see any plan of transportation adopted that can result in their being able to place manufactured goods in the west at cheaper rates than they can now be placed there. Now, in regard to tfhe question of the policy of past governments a most striking point doubtless is the large expenditure on the canal system, and I presume that I am within the mark when making the statement that $75,000,000, or even more, has been expended on the construction of the St. Lawrence and Welland canal systems, and according to the signs of the times large sums of money are to be expended by this government in still furthering these projects. While we are spending these large sums of money there is something which is withdrawn from the public to-day, and it is the idea of stability on the part of the government because members of the government are from time to time speaking of going farther in this, and of the possibility and chance that the government will take up other plans and projects with the view of ending this transportation question. So long as the government dangle before different sections of the provinces and the Dominion these gigantic projects, there can never be the possibility that the public will be assured that any plan is to be a permanent or lasting one for the future.
I am quite well aware of the fact that political considerations may in the past have weighed in some of these projects, but has the time not arrived when political considerations should be dropped, and even at the risk of offending the Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) and the Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) in this debate, I must say this, and say it ait the outset, that I fear and I think the public believe too, that too much heed is at present being paid to political considerations in the expenditures and in the expected expendi-

tures of vast sums1 of money in this country. We have in all lines of business a guiding star to lead people on and that is the success that others have attained in any particular project or enterprise of a similar kind, and looking to-day at the question of transportation, it must be plainly manifest to the world that the Americans in their route by way of Buffalo and New York by water from different points on the great lakes have seemingly achieved the solution of the transportation question. It is to be regretted that, while we in Canada have spent and are spending- millions of dollars on the St. Lawrence canal system year by year, we see with mortification that less grain is being shipped down this canal system upon which such large sums of money are being spent. Let me say, so far as this government are concerned, that if the St. Lawrence canal system is a failure, comparatively speaking, no blame is to be attached to the present government, because these gentlemen came into power finding a well-defined line of policy on the part of the late administration, and the present administration woidd have been blameable,
I believe, and would have been blamed by the country and by the press, had they not done exactly as they did, finding the work uncompleted and under tender, had they not gone on with the contracts that were then pending and completed the work as the work has been completed to-day. It is true that the government have claimed a great deal of credit in the past for the construction of this St. Lawrence canal system, while, as a matter of fact, they have simply carried on the lines of policy laid down by the late administration and whether it is a failure or success no blame can attach to the present administration, because the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals simply followed out the line of policy formulated by the late government. Last year this question was under discussion ; last year the lion. Minister of Railways and Canals had warning notes thrown out to him not only from this side of the House, but by his own political friends, but despite the warning notes then thrown out to the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals and the hon. Minister of Public Works, because, in their departments occur these great expenditures in this regard. these hon. gentlemen have still kept the public in a vacillating and doubtful frame of mind wondering what possible move is next to be made on the transportation checker board, so to speak, by this administration. While speaking from his place in this House the hon. member from North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton), who is not present to-day, made these remarks : Whether the building of the St. Lawrence canals was a mistake or not, and whether or not a heavy expenditure at Port Colborne is necessary, I think we have gone far enough in that direction until we have more reliable data as to effect of improvements in railways and reductions in cost of transportation by railways in Canada and the United States.
If that word of warning from the hon. member for North Norfolk was timely last year, how much more so is it to-day, in view of the
fact that the government have a great many plans and projects before the public asking for commendation and in due time I have no doubt parliament will be asked to sanction the expenditure not of hundreds of thousands of dollars but of millions. At the outset, I 'think there is a sort of mistaken idea in the minds of the people as to the extent of the trade which is to he assured to the Canadian system of transportation. At first sight it would seem that it is not a question of our reaching out simply for the Canadian trade or reaching out for a large portion of the trade of the United States. A glance at the map will show hon. gentlemen the fact that there is a certain area of the United States export trade which we in Canada may successfully hid for. We may, in Canada, hope, in time, to ensure this to our Canadian facilities and this has been demonstrated for two or three years beyond the possibility of a doubt. In this connection some figures may be interesting, which are compiled from the public reports to show the extent of the trade from certain American ports which we in Canada have a fair means of reaching out for by way of our Canadian schemes of transportation. At the port of New York I find from the figures of 1899 that there were exported no less a quantity than 93,830,352 bushels of grain. At the port of Boston there were exported 28,905,095 bushels of grain, and at the port of Baltimore 56,335,397 bushels. I have not the figures of the other American ports because I think that these are the only exporting points which we may hope to compete with to a certain extent.
Let us look for a moment at the vast trade that is done at the port of Buffalo. In the year 1899, the immense quantity of 153.393,1S4 bushels of grain passed through that port, and in addition to that there was handled at Buffalo, 40.899,928 bushels of grain in flour, or in all nearly 200,000,000 bushels. I have before referred to the superiority of the Buffalo system as shown by the immense trade that port does, compared with the relatively small quantity of grain passing through the St. Lawrence canal system, and which I regret to say is lessening year after year, compared with what is known as the Grand Trunk Railway and Canada Atlantic systems. The trade of Buffalo has largely increased in the last few years, owing to the fact that the railway and the shipping interests have worked hand in hand in modern improvements. There was a time on the great lakes, when a vessel carrying 20,000 or 25.000 bushels of grain was supposed to be of very considerable size, but that day lias gone past, and the grain freighter of the present time is a vessel carrying a quarter million bushels. Last year a vessel was launched at Cleveland, 'with a capacity of carrying 300,000

bushels of grain. A little consideration will show that that class of vessel is the one which has come to stay on the great lakes. These large vessels can be run at a comparatively less cost than the smaller ones, because the crew carried by the large vessels is not very much larger than that of the small vessels, while the expense of the higher class of officers is practically the same on both, i have seen on the lakes between Port Arthur, Chicago and Midland, a rate of live cents a bushel; so that a vessel carrying 300,000 bushels will earu $15,000 in freight, while the smaller vessel carrying 20,000 bushels will only earn the trifling sum of $1,000. It stands to reason that the demand should be for the large vessels, and the large vessels alone. I know that in the debate last year, there was a difference of opinion on that point between the hon. member for Quebec West (Hon. Mr. Ilobell), and the Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte). I am not here to decide between these two gentlemen, but in my humble opinion the signs of the times go to show that the hon. member for Quebec West was wrong in his contention. I believe that the time has not yet arrived for what may be termed canal freighters, but the day has certaiuly come for the larger class of vessels on the great lakes.
And, while they have been increasing the size of the vessels on the great lakes, the railways have not been idle by any means. There was a time when the railways between Buffalo and New York ran comparatively small trains, and with cars capable of carrying only GOO bushels; but I am credibly informed that to-day, there are cars on this railway system carrying 1,500 bushels, and locomotives which can each haul thirty of these large cars. A comparison can easily be drawn as to the very great saving which will be effected by the present railway system of doing business as against that of former days. There are many indications that the Buffalo grain trade is likely to increase. One reason is that there is always to be had cheap freight by boat between Buffalo, Duluth and Chicago. By reason of what are known as the coasting regulations, only these large American vessels can ply between Buffalo and Chicago, or any other American port on the great lakes. A Canadian vessel cannot trade between Buffalo and any American port, and so she is restricted to carrying between Buffalo and Port Arthur, or some other Canadian point. The result of that is that these American vessels are able to enter the ore carrying trade, which is now a very considerable factor in the United States, when the heavy grain trade of the spring is over. They leave the grain trade in the spring, and engage in the ore carrying trade during the summer months, and again in the fall they enter the grain carrying business. From time to time they are constructing more boats on the Ameri-Iv.tr. BENNETT.
can side, in view of the guarantee which they have that they will not only be able to engage in the grain trade in the spring and fall, but that they can carry ore during the summer months. There is another factor which militates against the grain carrying trade of Canada, and that is that ocean freight rates have been much cheaper from American ports than they have been from the ports of Montreal, St. John or Halifax. The reason is that there are always to be found a large number of ocean steamers in these American cities plying to European countries. In that respect the Buffalo grain trade has had a decided advantage in the past. The receipts of grain at Buffalo during the past year amounted to 57,000,000 bushels, from Chicago; 50,000,000 bushels from Duluth; 17,000,000 bushels from Milwaukee; 3,500,000 bushels from the Canadian port of Fort William, and the balance of 26,000,000 bushels fx'oiu other points, mainly on Lake Michigan. These figures show that the American people have been able to attract the bulk of the trade of the western states to the port of Buffalo, and not only that, but that they have been able to encroach on the Canadian trade from Port Arthur or Fort William to the extent of 3,500,000 bushels. This certainly should not be the case. With this condition of things staring us in the face, is it not time that we should take some measures to endeavour to cope with the enterprise of the American people, and to direct the current of trade into Canadian channels. We in this country, are to-day, largely relying on the canal system for this trade as the Americans relied on it in the past, but the Americans have changed their principle of doing business, and we can see for ourselves that the canal system is a failure.
Surely the time has arrived when this parliament, before it plunges into an expenditure of millions of dollars more through the government of the day, should adopt some fixed and definite policy, so that for a few years to come we may know where we are at. The grain trade of the west is going through Buffalo to the tune of nearly 200,000,000 bushels per year, while the grain trade at Montreal year after year is lessening. In the year 1898. 38,710,259 bushels of grain passed through the port of Montreal ; in 1899, 30.541,702 bushels passed through ; and in 1900, according to a computation which one must make, as the report of the Montreal Board of Trade does not show exactly what was carried in grain and what was carried in flour, only some 22,000.000 bushels must have passed through.	Unfortunately, we are not able to ascertain whether that grain went down the St. Lawrence canal system ; but, from all I can learn, instead of that quantity going down the canal system, less than 10.000.000 bushels actually passed down the St, Lawrence canals. The figures of the Canada At-

lantic show that that line handled some 13,000,000 bushels from Parry Sound to Montreal, which would leave only 9,000,000 bushels to go down by the St. Lawrence canals ; and the facts point to this being the case. While at Prescott and Kingston a large grain-handling trade has been done in past years, it is a regrettable fact that at Prescott no trade at all was done last year, and the trade of Kingston has diminished to a very appreciable extent. We have been attempting to build up the port of Montreal ; yet, after the large expenditure which we have incurred with that object, the truth must dawn on us that year by year, in spite of the deepening of the canal system from 10 feet to 14 feet, the grain trade of that port is very greatly diminishing.
It may be said that there are many reasons why the trade of the port of Montreal has not been built up. I am free to admit that that is so. In discussing this question with marine men and men conversant with the shipping trade, one hears that there is a great shortage of Canadian vessels. There will always be a shortage of Canadian vessels so long as the government continue to play fast and loose with this transportation question. What inducement is there for a man to-day to engage in Canadian shipping ? If he builds a Canadian bottom, he is restricted to the trade between Port Arthur and the port or Montreal, or Georgian Bay ports, whereas if he builds a vessel in the United States, he has not only tli,e grain trade between Buffalo and any point in the northern lakes to reiy upon, but he has during the summer months recourse to the vast ore trade, which is even a more profitable carrying trade than the grain trade. While the government are vacillating in their policy, vessel men hardly know what kind of vessel to build, if they are inclined to build a Canadian craft. They are told that the government intend to have the St. Lawrence canals so constructed as 1 to accommodate vessels going all the way from Port Arthur to Montreal. If you are going to have on that trade vessels with a capacity of 50,000 bushels, these are a class of vessels whicli cannot possibly compete with the larger vessels on the great lakes. In the same breath lion, gentlemen bespeak for use in Canada a class of vessels to carry grain from Port Arthur to Port Col-borne-Ayessels which are very much larger than those which have been projected.
There are some other points in Canada to which we have been attempting to attract trade ; and in this connection I am going to refer to Halifax and St. John. It must be remembered that every one of these plans of transportation that have been projected contemplate the expenditure of hundreds of thousands and even millions of dollars. What did we see last year ? The government of Canada had at Halifax a large grain elevator. The construction of that elevator, from all I can learn, had been
demonstrated to be practically a failure ; yet, in the face of that, the Minister of Railways and Canals saw fit in his wisdom, last year, to construct at St. John a large elevator, which, with the docks and wharfs and approaches, has involved an expenditure of half or three-quarters of a million dollars ; and I am sorry to say that one may fairly attribute to the hon. gentleman political I'easons for his action. What happened at that port last year ? The minister had his elevators and canals completed ; he had his railway system established to that point; yet, with that elevator standing there a monument, I will not say to his folly, but to his lack of business judgment, the Minister of Railways and Canals, in order to please the people of St. John, brings to that port, over the Canada Atlantic Railway to Montreal, and from there by the Intercolonial to St. John, 390,000 bushels of grain, to demonstrate that grain could be carried over that system of railways ; and the demonstration meant a loss to the revenue of Canada of $10,000. It is all very well to be patriotic ; it is all very well to build up a trade in the interest of the port of St. John ; but, surely the people of Canada are not to be asked to spend money at this rate simply to prove that the elevator at St. John has an adequate carrying capacity.
Now, looking at the canal system of the Dominion, we find from the experience of the past season, that the largest boat that passed from the upper lakes and went through to Montreal carried 45,000 bushels of grain ; and it is the opinion of practical vessel men to-day that it is utterly impossible to carry at a profit so small a quantity of grain so great a distance. What was the opinion of the hon. Minister of Railways last year on this question ? Speaking in this House, the hon. gentleman said :
We will see that with Montreal properly equipped, there is no reason in the world why we should not he able to offer sufficient inducements to shippers of grain in the west to prefer the St. Lawrence to any other route.
After a number of years, we find that the grain shipments at the port of Montreal have decreased to a most visible extent. Therefore, the opinion of the Minister of Railways last year was, I regret to say, rather a mistaken one. That hon. gentleman considered that one of the most desirable things in our canal system was this, that we would be able to carry through from points on the upper lakes heavy freight to Montreal, and to-day, with the deepening of the canal system, we find that last year the largest vessel that went down carried some 45,000 bushels. I am free to admit that the Welland canal to-day is only 14 feet deep, and that no doubt larger vessels should pass down that canal than those carrying 45,000 bushels. But there is this fact to be borne in mind. The Welland canal system is still water, and freighters

will not take the risk of carrying vessels deeply laden down the St. Lawrence that they would through the still water of the canal. But whether there are 14 feet or not in the' St. Lawrence system, I am informed that experience will prove that even with 14 feet, you can never hope to carry through vessels with much more than 50,000 bushels capacity. If you take vessels with 50,000 bushels from Fort William through to Montreal, you will find that they must of necessity return unloaded. There is no freight for vessels from Montreal to Toronto, or other points, to any appreciable extent. True, you may have freight for 'some of them, but not to any great extent, and the result is that boats are going back up the St. Lawrence system with comparatively little freight, and the more boats there are employed in that service the less quantity of return freight wall there be for each.
It was demonstrated in the past year by the Algoma Central Railway Company, that it will not- pay to send vessels right through from points on the lakes to the old country. They sent some boats over to the old country laden with steel billets, and the result was that these boats carried at a much less sum than paid their expenses, and the company were considerably out on the deal.
I need not go into the question of vessels leaving Fort William, and going clear to the old country. This proposition is so absurd that it does not require to be refuted. If you were to secure vessels capable even of carrying 00,000 bushels from Fort William to Liverpool, you would be brought into competition with the large first-class freighters fit Montreal; and could uot compete against the mixed cargoes and passenger lists on the ocean passenger vessels from the port of Montreal, so that transportation from the head of the great lakes through to Liverpool is a matter altogether out of the question.
Might I call the attention of the House to the fact that the lion. Minister of Railways and Canals has not been able to carry out the pledges he made last year as to the deepening of the St. Lawrence canal system. That is uot a matter anybody can find fault with. We can only regret it, but

Hon. gentlemen may say that it is all very well to offer criticism, but some solution should be suggested, and he who simply stands and complains ought not to be listened to. That experience has taught us that the people of the United States have laid down a definite line of policy. Their shipping interests, both by rail and water, have laid down the policy that you must construct on the great lakes the largest possible freighters, and have the most complete and modern means of railway communication. Well, I will deal now with that point which the minister has raised. I recall -the circumstance that two or three years ago the Minister of Railways spoke in the city of Halifax at a meeting of the board of trade, and he drew there what I believe was a truthful picture of the position of the transportation question in the country. He said : It is true, against the wishes of our political opponents, but in accordance with what we thought was the proper idea, we have now a means of communication from LSvis, which had hitherto been the termination of the Intercolonial Railway, clear through to the city of Montreal ; we have now a railway system from St. John and from Halifax to the port of Montreal, still I am free to confess, said the minister, we are in a very handicapped position. Our cars arrive at the city of Montreal and we find them empty. These cars we wish to take down to build up the trade of St. John and Halifax. As soon as we arrive at Montreal we are confronted with the fact that there are loaded cars there belonging to the Canadian Pacific Railway and to the Grand Trunk Railway. In our dilemma, he said, we approached the Grand Trunk Railway people and said to them : You have grain at Montreal, we wish to take that grain over the Intercolonial Railway system down to St. John or Halifax. The Grand Trunk Railway replied at once : AVe can carry our grain to Portland, which is some 300 miles shorter-I believe that was the distance-than the Grand Trunk Railway haul to St. John. As a result of that, he said, we are not able to secure from the Grand Trunk Railway Company a bushel of grain to carry down to the ocean. Now, he said, in our dilemma, we turned to the Canadian Pacific Railway and we asked them to give us the grain brought from the west to the port of Montreal. and the Canadian Pacific Railway replied to us : AVe have a shorter route to St. John than you have by the Intercolonial Railway, by some 300 miles. The result is.
said the hon. gentleman, that we have our empty cars at Montreal, and we are not able to get freight from the Grand Trunk Railway or from the Canadian Pacific Railway, and therefore we had nothing but failure staring us in the face.
Now, I think I have correctly stated the gist of the hon. gentleman's remarks in the city of Halifax on that occasion. But he went further at that time and outlined a policy on the part of the government, and that is the question which is to-day before the public. He said, there is a line of railway known as the Canada Atlantic Railway which runs from Montreal to a point on the Georgian Bay, to Depot Harbour. Now, he says, the policy of the government might be to acquire this line, and if we acquired that line we would have uninterrupted railway communication from a point on the Georgian Bay, by the Booth system, clear through to St. John or to Halifax, and then we would be in a position to bid for the grain trade ourselves. I think the minister will give me credit for stating correctly what he said on that occasion. But a sign of the times appeared later on. An hon. member who has the honour of representing the county of Hants (Mr. Russell) in this House, and who is accredited with holding a pretty prominent position in the House on the government side, came shortly afterwards to the rescue of the government and of the minister's line of policy, because there appeared from him in one of the Halifax newspapers a strong letter favouring the purchase of this Booth railway system. Now, I do not know whether the hon. member for Hants had the authority of the minister for formulating that policy for the government; but I do know that neither the Minister of Public Works nor the Minister of Railways and Canals will to-day stand up in the House and say that the government has not discussed, and that the government has not contemplated, the acquisition of what is known as the Booth line. Let me tell the Minister of Railways and Canals this, that it is in the mouths of the people east and west that that line is to be purchased by the government. Let me tell him more than this, that last winter when there was a good deal of discussion over the purchase of this road, a prominent personal friend who has the honour of sitting in this House, who is a gentleman of wealth, paid a flying visit to the town of Parry Sound and was looking around for real estate in that quarter. Surely that gentleman must have had an idea that the government were about to acquire the Booth line. So the minister is blowing both hot and cold. At one moment his government is going to buy out the Booth railway and throw the St. Lawrence system to the winds, and going to secure an uninterrupted railway communication clear through from a point on the Georgian Bay to a point on the Atlantic.

Perhaps the hon. gentleman will permit an interruption. I understand that to be the ground upon which he made the statement a few moments ago. Now, Sir, what is being done by the government to-day ? Here is the minister spending $2,000,000 at Port Colborne, and all that is to be brought about by this large expenditure will be simply that you will be able to transfer from a large boat into an expensive freighter on to Montreal; while if the minister had permitted affairs to go on as they have been going on, you might transfer at Kingston into cheaper boats, and the result would have been-as I am told by vessel men it will work out in the long run-that it would have been much better to go on with the old state of affairs. The hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) asked me what could be done under the circumstances ? In the first place, the gov-

ernment of tlie day through the Minister of Railways, told the people of Quebec, and told all these other people who had those baits held out before them, that the policy of the government is to adopt the St. Lawrence canal route system
Would the hon. gentleman please tell me what he means by 'bait' being held out before them ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Having baits held out before them. All I can say is that the minister, when he spoke at Halifax, told them the only advantage they ever could get in the carrying trade would be by the acquirement of the roads in the Booth system-
Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) venture to make such a statement as that seriously in this House ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I will say ' traffic arrangement ' if that suits.
I defy the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) to produce any statement that 1 ever made that will bear out his statement. I absolutely defy him.
speakername: The MINISTER OE RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Why, the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Blair) has said within a few minutes
I beg your pardon.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: You have not heard what I am going to attribute to you and you cannot know what it is

I do not know why the hon. gentleman should think that it is any advantage to him or to his party to misrepresent what I said. The hon. gentleman professed to give a statement which I made. I did not say that the only hope was to acquire the Booth system, but what I did say was : That one of the directions in which we hoped to get more business for the Intercolonial Railway was by having a traffic arrangement with the Booth lines, whereby we could exchange traffic. That is what I did say, but the hon. gentleman now puts it forward that I affirmed in Halifax that the only hope was to acquire the Booth system. I made no such statement at all.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. minister (Hon. Mr. Blair) held out to the people of Halifax the idea of a business arrangement-if that term will suit him-with the Canada Atlantic system. I state here that any business arrangement with the Canada Atlantic system by which you have to carry grain via the Georgian Bay, must be at the expense of the St. Lawrence canal system.

I do not see that.
33J
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I will refer to some facts that will perhaps convince the minister that the Booth system and the Grand Trunk Railway system from Midland have had the effect of diverting trade from the St. Lawrence canal system. We find that there are two well-defined lines of transportation in Canada, as against the St. Lawrence route. First, there is the Grand Trunk Railway system, which carries grain from its terminus at Midland on the Georgian Bay through to Montreal, and now, (thanks to the generous aid the government gave the Grand Trunk Railway in the matter of the Victoria bridge), on to Portland. The Grand Trunk Railway Company have been building up that trade, and they have been building it up successfully, and we find that in the past season, there was carried from Midland over their lines to Portland and to Montreal no less a quantity than 10,214,841 bushels.
Was there a bushel of that sent to Portland ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I think probably there was a portion of it.
Do you know it ? Have you any statement to that effect ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I am not in a position to know from the return whether a portion of that went to Portland or not.
Then why drag in the imputation that because we helped the Grand Trunk, therefore they got this business ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I am here to say that by reason of the fact that the government contributed so handsomely to the Grand Trunk to enable it to carry trade past Montreal, the Grand Trunk to-day are building up Portland, and I leave it to the hon. members from Montreal to say whether or not that is at the expense of Montreal.

That is altogether a different statement from that which the hon. gentleman made. The statement he made was that by reason of the assistance which the government had given the Grand Trunk for the bridge, they were carrying the grain which they received from the Parry Sound Railway, to Portland. Now, my information is that there is not a bushel of grain received by the Grand Trunk; from the Canada Atlantic Railway and taken to Portland.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If the minister makes the statement that none of the grain from Midland goes to Portland-
I am not talking about that. I am talking about grain received from the Parry Sound road.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The minister misunderstood me. The grain taken to Portland is from Midland, not from Parry Sound.
Then I was in error.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
The Grand Trunk bridge, by means of the half million dollars contributed by the government, has been so improved and strengthened that the Grand Trunk are to-day building at Portland an elevator with 2,000,000 bushels capacity. More than that, I know that the company which owns one of the large elevators at Midland is constructing at Chicago an elevator of 1,000,000 bushels capacity. My argument from that is that the Grand Trunk have every confidence that the carrying trade of this Dominion, not only from our own North-west, but from western points in the United States on the great lakes, will in future be done by way of Midland to Portland, with any trade which may incidentally enure to the port of Montreal ; and the result, I believe, will justify that confidence. It is, I believe, expected by the Grand Trunk Railway people that they will succeed in building up a very large trade.
Now, it is a fair question to ask, why can grain be successfully carried from Midland to Portland as against from Buffalo to New York ? There are many advantages in favour of the Midland-Portland system as 1 against the Buffalo-New York system. One of the first advantages is this, that you can make three trips from any point on the great lakes to Midland as against two trips to Buffalo, which is a very decided advantage, especially in the fall of the year ; so that a large vessel, with a capacity of from
200,000	to 300,000 bushels, would earn on that route from $10,000 to $15,000 more on three trips than if she went to Buffalo. That is the reason, I believe, why the Grand Trunk people are making preparations at Portland and at Chicago for a large carrying trade. The line of the Grand Trunk froth Midland to Belleville or Port Hope is poorly equipped ; they can only haul fourteen or fifteen cars, and those not of the largest size. When the day does arrive that the Grand Trunk has as complete a system of railways from Midland to Portland as there is from Buffalo to New York, there will be seen carried on that line, not 12,000,000 bushels of grain, but twice and probably three times that quantity.
I am not going to say anything in reference to the Parry Sound route. That route has asserted itself in the past year, and has shown that it is capable of carrying 13,000,000 bushels in a season. The other places on ! the lakes-Sarnia, Goderich and Colli ngwood -carried comparatively trifling quantities as compared with the systems from Parry | Sound to Montreal and from Midland to Portland.
Now, what is to be done under the circumstances ? " First, I say, in the very
words of this motion, a halt should be called on public expenditures. The government should at once drop the propositions which have been discussed before the public, by giving an official and authoritative denial of the statement that they have in contemplation the taking up of any of those propositions, and announcing that they intend in the future to pin their faith alone to the St. Lawrence canal system. When they do that, we shall have the satisfaction of seeing the vesselmen of the country embarking in the shipping interests of Canada.
If these railway systems, both the Grand Trunk and the Canada Atlantic, are able to compete with the Buffalo system, we may be sure that we can attract trade from Buffalo through Canada, which will be to the advantage of the Canadian public ; because every bushel of grain carried by vessel or by rail through Canada must be to the advantage of the Dominion as a whole, and more particularly to the advantage of the province' of Ontario through which it will pass ; and it is a debatable question to-day whether it would not be well for the government even to pay these people a bounty of so much a bushel for the grain -carried through Canadian channels for a year or so. The effect of giving such a bounty would be this, that they would be able to imi>rove their roadbeds to such an extent that, I believe, they would cut appreciably into the Buffalo trade.
In conclusion, I have only to say that I have introduced this resolution, as I did last year, hoping that it would evoke some little discussion-hoping that any views thrown out in the debate-not any poor views of mine-would be taken up by the press and discussed, and that the gentlemen sitting behind the government and retaining them in their position would be moved, in a spirit of patriotism, to ask themselves : Is there any means that can be adopted for increasing the grain trade through Canada- not only our own trade, but by taking part of the trade now going through the United States 1 I believe the solution of the whole question rests on this-that some encouragement should be given both to the Canada Atlantic system and to the Grand Trunk system, provided they carry a largely increased quantity of grain over what they are now carrying. But, above all things, here and now is the place and time for the Minister of Railways and Canals, before this debate closes, to announce that the government intend for the future, at least for a fixed period of five or six years, to pin their faith to the St. Lawrence canal system, and not introduce any of the side schemes or projects which are now before the public.
Mr. Speaker, I must offer my congratulations to the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) for having so fully drawn the

attention of tlie House to this important ' question. I do not think there has been a matter brought before the House this ses- ; sion of more importance than this question of transportation ; and in congratulating the hon. gentleman upon having brought it to our attention, I wish I could also compliment him upon the accuracy of his statement of the case. But, I regret to say, he made many grievous mistakes. There were many causes operating against the removal of grain to Montreal last year on which he did not even touch. And 1 am quite sure that when these exceptional causes are brought before the House, hon. members will at once understand why there was not more grain brought down the St. Lawrence last year.
I confess that I read the motion of the hon. gentleman with some degree of doubt, because I could not quite see what it was intended to cover. He says that it is now time this government should state its policy in this matter. But I do not think that the government has ever withheld from this House the policy it was intending to pursue. The government has acted upon the policy that every possible avenue that could be utilized for the transportation of grain and other produce, not only from our own great North-west, but also from the north-western states, should be taken advantage of and improved, and I do not care whether those improvements are confined to water navigation alone or extended to a combination of water and rail. We all know that if we depend simply on our water navigation, we will be shut off during the winter months from a very large supply of grain, and,
. therefore, it is desirable that we should make provision ahead by establishing large storehouses at different points. My hon. colleague, the Minister of Railways and Canals, was fully justified in the large expenditure he undertook at Port Colborne. To use the hon. gentleman's own argument, we will be able to bring to Port Colborne steamers drawing 20 feet of water and carrying grain to the extent of 200,000 bushels, and certainly 150,000 bushels, and that grain can be transhipped thence in barges and steamers, not merely carrying 45,000 bushels, as mentioned by the hon. member for Bast Simeoe (Mr. Bennett), but 200,000 bushels, for I maintain that a steamer and two consorts can bring down from Port Colborne
200,000	bushels, and even more. As I figure it out, two barges and a steamer would be able to bring 210,000 bushels from Port Colborne, and we have been told by a most reputable and trustworthy shipbuilder in the west, that that will prove the most economical way of moving grain from Port Colborne or Port Arthur or Duluth or any other point to the seaboard.
The hon. member for Bast Simeoe dwelt at considerable length on what the port of Buffalo has done. But how has Buffalo managed to do what it has accomplished ?
That port obtained command of the grain trade simply through our supineness in years gone by. While we made the Sault Ste. Marie canal 20 to 22 feet deep, and the Welland canal 14 feet deep, when the grain got into Lake Ontario it was shut out from the St. Lawrence canal, because our locks and canals there would not carry vessels drawing 10 feet of water. The greatest draught that could get through the St. Lawrence canals was about 6, 7 or 8 feet, and, under the most favourable conditions, never more than 8 feet. What, therefore, are we doing '! We passed through our ' Soo ' canal 4 000,000 tons of American shipping the year before last entirely free of toll, and then gave it to Buffalo. Why ? Because there was no other place to receive it. Therefore, the government took in hand the work at Port Colborne, in order that that port might accommodate these large steamers, even as large as 6,000 tons, and from there the grain would be reshipped to Montreal, or Quebec or elsewhere. The hon. gentleman laid great stress on the probability of our killing the trade of Kingston and Prescott and other places by these improvements at Port Colborne. But he is not able to see far enough. If we are to get any proportion of our western trade, we shall have a trade not only for our Welland canal and our water navigation-which, I believe, will in the main be the most economical way of moving our crops-but it is probable that our railways will be utilized in order to bring the grain through much quicker, even though it cost a little more. But, as regards the bulk of the grain, I believe there are no advantages on the American side over our St. Lawrence and great lakes. We should not belittle our advantages, but should instead show to the people of the whole continent that our ports of Montreal and Quebec will not only be national ports, but great international ports for the transhipment of grain in ocean steamers, and also for the , transhipment of products from England to the far west.
The hon. gentleman also laid some stress upon the quantity of grain that could be carried through our canals to Montreal, and very much underrated it. He said that no : vessel had brought more than 45,000 bushels through last yaer.

I must say this, that that 1 was in reply to a question I asked the Min. ister of Railways and Canals.
i Hon. Mr. DOBELL. I am not saying that
*	the hon. gentleman was not correct in his - statement of quantity, but what was the ; cause of that ? It was simply this, that i there were so many detractors of the work
*	of deepening the St. Lawrence canals to 14 feet that the report was circulated broadt cast that such work had not been accom-C plished, and to-day you will find some people i arguing that it is not jjossible to bring ves-? sels drawing 14 feet of water through the

St. Lawrence canals. But my hon. colleague, the Minister of Railways and Canals,
gave us the assurance a few days ago that there is not the slightest risk or danger to barges or steamers going through our St. Lawrence canals drawing 14 feet of water. The hon. gentleman also forgot entirely the very abnormal state of things which existed last year. We could not get steamers to go up the St. Lawrence. I pointed out two years ago the discrimination that existed in our insurance rates, and if those rates cannot be amended, the Grand Trunk Railway have acted wisely in taking their grain to Portland, where they ship at less than one-third the insurance rates charged -from the St. Lawrence. This is far more serious than people imagine.
I believe it is the duty of the government and of every member of this House to do all they can to have that remedied. I do not believe that there is any good cause for the discrimination that has taken place. If the hon. member for East Simcoe had really thought out the subject carefully and wanted to put a fair case before the country, he should have given the government his assistance by pointing out what steps should be taken to have this insurance matter put right. I believe that for all these years we have been debarred from using the St. Lawrence in the winter or as early in the spring as we might. I believe, for my part, in absolute winter navigation, that we have nothing like the difficulties that Russia is now combatting, both in the Black Sea and in the Baltic, in the matter of ice. There may be a time in the middle of March, and perhaps up to the early part of April, when in the gulf the northern ice blocks the channel between Cape Ray and the Bird Rocks. But that happens only once in three or four years, perhaps not so often. But the matter of snow storms is very much exaggerated. It is true we have snow storms on the lower St. Lawrence, and all along the valley of that river as well. But, you have snow storms in the English channel, which render navigation there very dangerous because of the number of steamers navigating those waters. But we have good anchorage in the St. Lawrence, for from the time you enter the river up to Quebec, there is no difficulty when a storm comes on in anchoring and waiting until it is over. A snow storm does not last, ordinarily, for more than twenty-four hours. So, there is no such reason for this discrimination against the St. Lawrence as is alleged. If we could establish winter navigation in Quebec, and make Quebec a great emporium for trade by building large elevators, a great step in advance would be taken. And I believe that the Grand Trunk will find that they have made a serious mistake in going to Portland, because you can carry grain from Montreal to Quebec for less than half what you can carry it

for from Montreal to Portland. So, if this insurance question is challenged and remedied, as I believe it will be by the government, we shall do more for St. Lawrence navigation than has ever been done before. The hon. member for East Simcoe said that I had told the House that the proportion of the grain trade carried through the St. Lawrence river never exceeded 8 per cent. I am not quite sure that it ever reached 8 per cent, but that is very near it. The hon. gentleman says I said that in 1901 it would be 25 per cent. I have not had the opportunity of consulting * Hansard,' but my recollection is that I said that we ought to have 25 per cent, and that we will get 25 per cent, but I do not think I limited the acquiring of this 25 per cent to one year.

Before the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Dobell) leaves the question of insurance, which is a very important one, and one on which, I am sure, the House desires to be informed, can he give me the figures of the amounts paid to the underwriters for insurance on the St. Lawrence and the losses to those same underwriters.
Shillings ?
What about Montreal ?

I would not belittle
Montreal at all. Montreal has incurred very heavy expenditure in deepening Lake St. Peter and they deserve credit for it. At that time Quebec was asleep, but now we have wakened up a little, we see our advantages, and we hope to utilize them to such an extent that there will be shipped from Quebec, not merely 25 per cent of the grain which I mentioned twelve months ago, but a very much larger proportion. I believe that this government, by its policy of improving every avenue of shipment, will ultimately increase very greatly grain shipments at the port of Quebec. I do not know' much about the Georgian Bay canal, but if opening it up to North Bay will give us increased advantages for getting grain down, I'will go in for it. I do not think the result will be what the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) fears, that is, to rob our St. .awrenee canals of their trade, because there will be more grain to carry than the St. Lawrence canals can handle, and all the railways you can build. We are not able to realize the possibility that lies before this Canada of ours. We ought to have more faith in our future than to think that by improving Port Colborne we are going to ruin the trade at Kingston. I am sorry the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Britton) is not in his place, because I do not think he would share in the fear of ruining Kingston. I presume there will be trade enough for all possible routes. Instead of getting forty million bushels, or fifty million bushels down the St. Lawrence canals, we want to get that two hundred millions that is going now by Buffalo, or a large share of it. Certainly, we ought to get all our Manitoba wheat. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that next year the hon. member for Simcoe will be able to change his tone a little, and have a little more faith in the government and in the St. Law'rence route.

I shall not say much on this subject, because I do not profess to have that intimate knowledge of the internal transportation of grain which some hon. gentlemen opposite seem to have, and which every person ought to have in dealing with a subject of this nature. But I am encouraged by the remarks that have fallen from some hon. gentlemen in this

House wlio have made long and strong arguments containing the scantiest modicum of intelligence on the subject. Now, *Mr. Speaker, if there is any subject which the Liberal-Conservative party placed before the inhabitants of Nova Scotia and of the lower provinces generally, it was the prospect that by means of the railway system of Canada, and by means of the improved transportation, our ports would be made the point of shipment for immense quantities of produce from the west on the way to Europe. If I understood the argument of the hon. member for Simcoe it was that the quantity transported by water and by rail to the port of Montreal this year was very much less than in previous years, and from that fact he deduced the ' argument that the means which the government had provided for transporting the grain were not successful, were not proper. Now, I have been led to understand that there was less grain produced in the North-west during the past year than in previous years, and that would account for the fact that less grain was shipped from the port of Montreal, and therefore the long and laboured argument of the hon. gentleman directed against the government would fall to the ground.
Moreover, the hon. gentleman must know that tlie carriage by steamers of different kinds on the lakes does not cover the whole transportation question. He should be able to tell us what proportion the cost of lake carriage bears to the cost of the transportation of grain between the terminal points, that is to say, between the point of production in the west and the point of shipment in the east, wherever that may be. The small cost on a portion of the route may be balanced by advantages on the longer portion of the route, and that would destroy the value of the hon. gentleman's argument. I do not know what the exact amount of toll is between the point of production and Buffalo, or those other ports on the lakes. But there are other considerations, after the grain has reached the place of shipment, and those considerations are connected with the question of Atlantic navigation. We have heard something this afternoon about the tempestuous character of navigation on the lakes, that vessels cannot navigate the lakes with masts. Well, Sir, do modern vessels navigate the great Atlantic ocean with masts ? The great steamers on the Atlantic all dispense with their masts, they do not depend upon sails at all. but entirely upon steam power. Now, if large vessels are to be employed to carry this grain after it has reached the point of shipment, the larger the vessel employed on the longer portion of the route the greater will be the profit of the shipper. I say there is no port in Canada, there is no port in the United States, there is no port in the western world, which affords better

facilities for the shipment of grain across the Atlantic than the port of Halifax.
Perhaps some hon. gentleman may think that I am an amateur on this subject, as some sceptical people thought the other day that I was an amateur on the subject of farming. I know something about the subject of navigation also. Into the port at Halifax there come the largest steamers in the world. I was on board two of the largest steamers in the world in Halifax, one the steamer Pennsylvania, of the Ham-burg-American line. This, the largest ship in the world, came into Halifax without a pilot, and the captain turned her around himself, under my direction, and went out again without a pilot, showing the superior navigating facilities of that port. Now, Mr. Speaker, there is this point, and it is the solution of this question of navigation : We know that the tramp steamers, those that carry the grain in bulk, and nothing else, are the vehicles of communication which make the rates on grain. You cannot bring them up to Quebec or to Montreal in the winter time. They go to ports in the United States because the grain is collected there for them, and they go to those ports in ballast. What is the great difficulty of winter navigation ? It is that these ships have to come out from England or continental points empty, and that is the great difficulty of winter navigation, as the captains tell me. I only repeat what a number of them have told me. They say : We can get no cargo to bring out to United States ports, and we have to depend on the back freight to make the enterprise pay. Here is the solution of it : Bring out the western trade, bring out the freight from England and other ports to Halifax in these steamers and the whole question is solved. You will have back freights which will reduce the rate on grain one-third or one-half, and there is no other port in Canada to which you can bring those back freights. What about the winter navigation of the St. Lawrence ? Did they not try to run a steamer from Paspebiac to Europe, and what was the report we got ? Steamer still in sight, still in the ice ; a week later, relief steamer gone out, steamer still in the ice ; at the end of a month, steamer still in the ice, steamer in sight, and relief steamer in the ice. They will always be in the ice, and they will always remain there while the St. Lawrence goes out, while the Arctic ocean is to the north, and while the Atlantic is beyond. Hon. gentlemen may talk about intermediate points upon the lakes, about one point on Lake Erie and another point on Lake Ontario, but the only solution is to get down to deep water on the Atlantic. Political parties have been trifling with the question all along. An hon. gentleman said that there was an elevator at Halifax. There was an elevator at Halifax, and grain was shipped through that elevator, but

through the carelessness of the Conservative party the elevator was burned down. There is an elevator at Halifax now, a beautiful, capacious elevator, with every facility adapted to the movement of grain. It only requires the grain to be brought there when the superior advantages of the port of Halifax will be at once demonstrated. What keeps it back 1 Why is not the experiment made ? Is it the timidity of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, or is it owing to the lack of rolling stock to transport the grain which is ready to go over the railway ? I am told it is the absence of rolling stock, the paucity of locomotives, and a great many other detrimental circumstances which prevented the experiment being tried.
In regard to insurance upon the St. Lawrence, I may say that amongst my other qualifications, I was 21 years in an insurance office, and I know that the insurance companies who want to make money very shrewdly conjecture where the risk is which calls for these high premiums, and they know that the navigation of the channel of the St. Lawrence from the month of October is very dangerous. In the summertime, with a certain depth of water, the St. Lawrence is good enough, but for all seasons of the year, for all depths of water and all sorts of tonnage, there is no port in the world, certainly not on the western hemisphere, that can compare with the port of Halifax. There is another rival springing up, and a rival with which the St. Lawrence will have to struggle, perhaps in the summer time, perhaps in the winter time. I am informed by the captains of these ships which carry grain, that desperate efforts are being made to make New Orleans the terminus of the grain-carrying trade, and that the navigation of the Mississippi is going to be the great rival of the St. Lawrence. They have prepared their elevators, they have a variety of products to give a variety of cargoes, and they believe that they can successfully compete with any means of communication possessed by us ; but, in the meantime, until the question of these rival ports is settled, we must have some outlet for the trade of Canada, and the problem will not be successfully solved except by means of back freights from Europe, which will lessen the rates of freight, coupled with the use of the free port of Halifax, with all those facilities which are necessary to enable the produce to be handled at a cheap rate, and which will prevent the trade from going by any other route.

Mr. Speaker, a good deal has been said by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Roche) in support of that very valuable port, and a good deal has been said by the hon. minister without portfolio ! (Hon. Mr. Dobell) in favour of Quebec. ] Every person seems to have forgotten that i
there is a little place called Montreal. There have certainly been solutions offered both by the hon. minister without portfolio and by the hon. member for Halifax, but I do not think that we have quite yet arrived at the solution of the difficulty. It is a very simple one to my mind, and I think the Board of Trade of Montreal, a very important body, as well as the Board of Trade of Toronto, have made known to the government just what they think would be the solution of the difficulty. The solution of the difficulty would be a safe 14-foot channel from the west to the foot of Laehine canal, a safe 30-foot channel, 500 feet wide, from the foot of Laehine canal to the ocean, and having these channels lighted so that steamers could proceed as well by night as by day, as they do in other countries and in the ports to the south of us.- The hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) has stated that the grain export trade from Montreal and the shipping have fallen off considerably in the last few years. I think he is slightly in error about that. It is true that during 1899 there was not as much produce exported as in 189S. That,
I believe, was owing to the fact that we could not get steamers last season, because many of the very best of our steamers were taken by the British government for transport service to South Africa, and that diminished the tonnage out of Montreal. There was no very serious falling off, however. In the year 1899, there were 30,000,090 bushels of grain shipped from the port of Montreal, and 39,000,000 bushels was the highest point ever reached. Last year a larger number of inland vessels arrived at the port of Montreal, but there was a falling off in the ocean steamers. In 1S98, 830 ocean-going steamers arrived in Montreal, and in 1899, only 771. That falling off, as I have said, was largely due to the vessels being engaged by the British government in the war service.
I may say, Mr. Speaker, that I have had considerable difficulties at times with the Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte), but I am happy to say that he had grasped the situation on the present occasion and solved tiie problem by affording us a thirty-foot channel, 500 feet wide in the St. Lawrence river. If the Minister of Marine aud Fisheries (Hon. Sir Louis Davies) will now do his part, and have our navigable waters down there lighted and buoyed to the same extent as are the American ports, then we will certainly get the insurance rates reduced. The hon. gentleman from Quebec West (Hon. Mr. Dobell) expressed the wish that we had a responsible Canadian marine insurance company in this country. I can tell the hon. gentleman that we have such a company. We have the Western Assurance Company of Toronto, than which there is no better or more reliable assurance company in the world. I might mention that the hon. member for Toronto Centre (Mr. COMMONS
Brock) is one of the directors of that company, and the Hon. Senator Cox is president. I can tell the House that the experience of that company during the last ten years has been that they have paid out three dollars for every dollar they have received. In view of that, how can we expect lower insurance. An hon. gentleman spoke about the Clergue steamers going down the St. Lawrence last fall. I remember the circumstances very well. The steamers were delayed somewhere up the lakes, and they went through from Montreal after the buoys had been moved from the channel, because the buoys must be removed from Lake St. Peter before the ice takes, or they cannot be removed at all. These four Clergue steamers went down, and one of them came to grief. I do not know whether or not that is the one the hon. gentleman referred to as being insured, but at all events some one of them came to grief and was obliged to go into dry dock at Halifax. Now, I would point out to hon. gentlemen that it will not take a very great deal of money to put our navigable waterways in first-class condition. The only fault we have to find with the Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) is that he does not ask for sufficient money in his estimates, and I can tell the minister, and I can tell the House, that if Canada is ever to be made commercially great, now is the time to do it. I repeat that it will not take a great deal of money to carry out this very important work, and the present is the time to do it or not at all. A great many of our friends, especially the Board of Trade of Montreal, are much exercised over the fact that the Grand Trunk Railway has made its terminus at a foreign port. Well, Sir, I am of opinion that that is not altogether an unmixed evil, because I believe the result of it will be that both political parties will be spurred on to a supreme effort to protect the trade of Canada, so that in the end good will result. The hon. members who represent the province of Manitoba will bear me out in the statement that out of the 56,000,000 bushels of grain annually shipped from the North-west, less than 15 per cent of it goes through Canada, and 85 per cent of the whole export goes through United States territory and from United States ports. There is no patriotism in business-except in a few cases at least-and if a man can ship his grain from Manitoba to Great Britain and save $8,000 or $10,000 a year by sending it through a foreign port, he is going to do it. What we have to do in this country, and what we have to do now, is to make our facilities for transportation so cheap and so good that we shall have all our grain and all other exports from Canada going through our own country and shipped from Montreal or Quebec, or from the maritime provinces in the winter.

When I mention Quebec, I do so because I know that in Montreal we are too broadminded to have any jealousies. We recognize that what is good for Quebec is good for the rest of the country, and that if Quebec prospers, then Montreal and Toronto, and our other Canadian cities will prosper too.
In my opinion the hon. gentleman from Bast Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) has not proposed the right solution of the difficulty. I believe that the Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) is on the right course, and if he succeeds in carrying out these improvements there will be no question but that the insurance rates will be reduced. As I see the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Sir Louis Davies) in his seat, I would make a suggestion to him which I consider of great importance. I do trust that he will supply a steamer next winter to keep the ice broken at Cap Rouge. It is well known to the hon. Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte), and to the hon. member for Quebec West (Hon. Mr. Dobell) that the ice at Cap Rouge sometimes attains a thickness of forty feet.
Sixty feet.

I accept the hon. gentleman's amendment. Now that we have started to build the Quebec bridge at this very spot, the piers and abutments of that bridge will certainy have the effect of causing the ice to be thicker still.
Oh, no ; the contrary.

Well, we will have to differ on that point. I believe that the effect of the bridge will be to keep the ice there longer and later in the spring. While I am not as sympathetic as my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Dobell) is towards the idea of having navigation all the year round, I do believe that if the Minister of Marine and Fisheries would provide a steamer to keep the Cap Rouge ice broken we would have navigation at least ten or fifteen days earlier in Montreal, and I think the experiment would be well worth while making. My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Dobell) is very strong on winter navigation, and I hope he will succeed. I trust Quebec may succeed in having winter navigation, but I have grave doubts that even if you do keep the river open between Quebec and the gulf, that you will get any one to use it. Steamers would have to come up there through severe snow storms, and I am afraid the insurance of the underwriters would be so high as to render navigation during the winter months well nigh impracticable.
Before the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bickerdike) sits down, I would like to ask him whether he claims that there is not a fourteen-foot channel on the St. Lawrence route down to Lachine.

The difficulty to my mind is this. I believe there is fourteen feet of water, but the impression has gone out that fourteen feet of water means a fourteen-foot channel, and that a vessel drawing fourteen feet of water could come down safely through that. That is an impossibility. Fourteen feet of water would only mean, to my mind, a thirteen-foot channel, because a vessel must have one foot of water under her keel to navigate with any degree of safety.
Fourteen feet, on the mitre sills is what is claimed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That would pass a vessel drawing 134 feet safely.

Mr. Speaker, before the motion is put, I wish to say a few words on this question which interests to a very considerable extent a portion of the county which I have the honour to represent. The motion as it reads, strikes me as being peculiar in its terms. It says :
That in the opinion of this House, the time has arrived when a fixed and definite line of action should be undertaken on the question of transportation of the grain and other commodities of the North-west Territories, Manitoba and the western states, with a view to centreing the same to the greatest possible extent in Canadian channels.
Well, Sir, if no fixed idea had been arrived at, I would think that the time had certainly come when a fixed and definite line of action should be taken, but to my mind a fixed and definite line of action was adopted many years ago. It was adopted by the Conservative party when in power, and it has been followed up, and followed up properly and to greater advantage to the country by the present government. That fixed line of action was that we should open up the country to bring about as far as possible the transportation of the western products of Canada to the seaboard by means of our water communication. That was the policy of the Conservative party when they enlarged the Welland canal.
But, Sir, this line of action has been exceeded by the present government. They are not only carrying out the line of policy adopted by hon. gentlemen opposite when in power, but they are going further, to this extent, that they are deepening our harbours and opening every means of communication from the west to the east; and that is the proper line of policy to pursue. Whether It may affect Midland or Port Col-borne or Parry Sound has nothing whatever to do with the question. The question is, shall we open up every line of communication from the west to the east in this country, so that the products of the west shall be carried through Canadian channels to the seaboard, and not through American channels ? That is the policy which should be adopted, and that is the policy which has been adopted. If the hon. gentleman's resolution is an insinuation that such a policy has not been adopted, then, I say it should not pass this House. There should not go forth to the public the suggestion that there is not a definite line of policy with reference to the transportation of the products of this country to the seaboard.
It is said that we are not carrying the quantity of the products of the west that we should carry. It was stated by an hon. member from Montreal (Mr. Bickerdlke), who has had a wide experience in this line of business, that last year about 85 per cent of the wheat grown in our own North-west Territories was carried to the seaboard through American channels. That is a lamentable state of affairs, and we want to remedy it. The policy of this government is, I understand, to endeavour to remedy that state of affairs.
It is said we are not carrying to the seaboard the quantity of the products of the west which go through American channels. Is not the riddle easy to read ? Why, it is only a few years since we had a North-west. It is only a few years in the life of a country that we have had a homogeneous, united Dominion. It was only a few years ago that this Dominion was born. Prior to that time, though the Welland canal was built to some extent, there was not that united and energetic effort to acquire for the whole length and breadth of this country the mercantile supremacy to which this country is entitled. It was split up into disorganized communities-the provinces down by the sea, the North-west unexplored and unknown, Upper Canada a considerable country, Lower Canada a considerable country, but the different parts with divergent interests, and not working together along the one line of building up a great and united country. When confederation was brought about, these provinces were united, and then we began to see that what would be for the benefit of one section of this Dominion would make for the interests of the whole, whether it might be Montreal or Quebec, Midland or Port Colborne. Since then the North-west Territories have been joined to this Dominion, and now the products of that great North-west are pouring down to the seaboard to the open market in Europe. Who is to carry those products ? Are they to go through American or Canadian channels ? Are we to fill up that country with a hardy, intelligent and prosperous population, producing enormous quantities of grain and other commodities for the markets of the world, and are those supplies to go through Canadian territory ? The object of this government, I understand, and I trust to support them in carrying it out, is to develop every line of transportation which can be developed to bring those commodities through our own territory.

The hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) made a very lengthy speech. He complained about everything in general, but nothing in particular. My reputation may have preceded me, though I doubt if that reputation is one of obtuseness ; but I must be exceedingly obtuse, for I could not grasp what the hon. gentleman was driving at. He gave us no suggestion of a remedy for the evils whiidh he claims exist, of (there be evils. He simply expressed the opinion that the Grand Trunk Bail-nay and the Canada Atlantic Railway should be bonused by the government in order to induce them to carry grain in competition with the very route which he says the government should pin its faith to. 1 failed to apprehend the argument of the hon. gentleman In any particular. He does not propose a remedy. He launches out with the statement that some member of the government made a speech in some section of the country that did not correspond with a speech made by some other member of the government in another section. I venture to say that there has not been a speech made by any member of the government in any section which has not been in the direction of developing the transportation facilities of this Canada of ours. The Welland canal has been talked of. The expenditure at Port Colborne has been talked of. Did not the Conservative party, when in power, spend millions of dollars in enlarging the Welland canal. Their policy was a mistake, for this reason, that the class of vessels now plying on the upper lakes could not go into Port Colborne, by reason of the low water there. Those vessels go to Buffalo, because they are obliged to go there. They will go to Port Colborne and tranship the products of the North-west in tow barges to Montreal as soon as the harbour is deepened to 22 feet ; and that is what the government is doing at the present time. I heard the suggestion made that the Welland canal should be enlarged to a greater depth, and that the transhipment should take place at Kingston. The hon. gentleman proposed something of that kind this afternoon. He does not propose that it should be the policy of the government, so that the larger vessels on the upper lakes could go to Kingston.
He cries a halt.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
He cries a halt.' He thinks they should go to Midland. Probably the government will enlarge the harbour at Midland. At the present time I think the policy of enlarging the Welland canal would be a mistake. Let us deepen the harbour at Port Colborne so that the same class of vessels can go there as go to Buffalo, and can tranship their cargoes at Port Colborne as they tranship their cargoes at Buffalo. The distance from Port Colborne to the seaboard is nearly 500 miles shorter than from Buffalo to the seaboard.
When that is done, let us look around and see if there is not a means of bringing about the result we are striving for. There is one thing which has been to some extent a drawback, and that is the failure to get a return cargo. That is one of the drawbacks with which Canadian shipping has to contend. Ships go to Buffalo with a cargo of wheat or to Cleveland or Erie with a cargo of iron ore, and they go back with a cargo of coal. But anthracite coal is on our free list, and it can be laid down at the port of Colborne and shipped from that port just as readily as from Buffalo. It can be brought to Port Colborne just as cheaply as to Buffalo, and I believe there is sufficient enterprise in this country to bring about a condition of affairs which will give these large vessels return cargoes from Port Colborne to the west, and thus build up the great trade that should be ours.
I do not know that I have anything more to say on the question. The resolution is a peculiar one, and one hardly knows whether it should pass or not. It insinuates that the government of this country has not had, on this question, a definite line of policy. But that statement is utterly unfounded. The government has a definite line of policy, one which I approve, and one which I believe both sides of the House will be glad to see carried out-a policy which will build up this country, irrespective of whether the port of Montreal or Quebec or Port Colborne or Midland are specially benefited or not, and a policy which will aid in making this Dominion the great and glorious country we all desire it should be.
