House in Committee on Bill (No. 7) respecting the Grand Trunk Railway of Canada.-Mr. Geoffrion.

I shall not take up the time of the committee at any length, but wish simply to call attention to the character of liis measure. It is a Bill legalizing a transaction between the Grand Trunk Railway and an American railway company, by which the Grand Trunk Railway assumes responsibility for a railway in the United States, which has been making deficits for years, that have been met by increased charges put upon the traffic in Ontario. I rise to enter my protest against this House endorsing any such arrangement between the Grand Trunk Railway and a corporation outside this country.
It is very apparent to me, from the remarks I have just heard, that facts are things which cut no material figure with the hon. gentleman.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS (Hon. A. G. Blair).

speechtext:
1049 MAUCH 6, 1901 * 1050	
The hon. gentleman was present at a meeting of the Railway Committee when this Bill was considered and disposed of. There was no division upon it. The statements that were made hy several members of that committee made it abundantly clear that there was not sufficient ground upon wliiidh the committee could refuse to report the Bill favourably to the House. Two or three of the leading facts, I may say the strongest possible evidential facts, were those : That there was, in 1878, an Act passed by this parliament which conferred in express terms upon the Grand Trunk Railway the right to acquire or make arrangements by leasing or otherwise, or make tr." i'c arrangements of any kind, with any radway with which it desired to be connected n the United States. There was no limitation whatever upon that power. That passed in 1878. I think it was only a year from that date when the government of this country, supported and approved by parliament, imposed as a condition upon its purchase of a portion of the Grand Trunk line-I mean the portion between Levis and Rivi&re du Loup-that it should go outside of the territory of Canada and expend its resources in making railway connection between Detroit and Chicago. It imposed that charge upon the Grand Trunk Railway. Later than this, and in respect of this road which is now in question, in 1890, the Grand Trunk Railway Company made a leasing contract with that company, which leasing contract was submitted to parliament and was approved. Now, they are not making a new contract at all with the company. They are revising the terms under which the other arrangement was made, and as the facts were presented to us, it is made abundantly clear that they were making a beneficial arrangement for themselves, and that the proposals were of a nature which from a business point of view, could not be other than approved. And the only obligation, apparently that they were assuming by this arrangement which was at all different from their previous existing contract with the company was an arrangement to pay a sum as rental amounting to $43,000 a year. This was not in addition, as I would gather from the facts, to their previous obligation in respect of this road, but it put the form of a specific rental when they were taking over and re-issuing in another form, certain bonds with certain guarantees which were associated with the transaction. Now, it is said that it is wrong for the Grand Trunk Company to go to the United States and acquire any of these roads. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) puts his objection to this Bill upon that ground. It might be a very wise conclusion for parliament to arrive at to say that we will not sanction any arrangement of this kind which the Grand Trunk Company might make as respects railways outside of Can-	ada from this time forward. I am not going to say that I would feel that there would be any public interest that parliament would serve by coming to such a conclusion ; but I can understand that there might be gentlemen who have extreme views with regard to these matters who might entertain that opinion. I would not quarrel with that opmion now-the time has not come to deal with it. But it is manifestly clear that we are not in a position to treat this proposal as a new one or one that has had no legislative sanction or no reason for existence. Tthe reverse is the fact. I can scarcely believe that the hon. gentleman has considered this matter. It seems to me that he must think that there is a little kudos, a little political prestige to be got out of jumping up and opposing, whether on tenable grounds or not, a proposition of this kind. I am sure if the hon. gentleman were called upon to take the responsibility of actually giving effect to the intention he has declared of defeating this, he would not take that responsibility. I am well assured of that. There was no member of the committee so far as I coud gather, except the hon. gentleman himself, who had any doubt that. this was a proper Bill to pass. It passed in committee nem con. Mr. MACLEAN. I have called attention to a practice which is growing and which the Minister of Railways himself, In a committee, yesterday pointed out as a dangerous one, so far as regards a similar Bill before the committee. I am well within my right in doing what I have done, the hon. minister will find other things happening that will justify what I am doing. Even if there was this general power given to the road of which the hon. minister speaks, surely parliament has retained discretionary power over any special application under that general power that may come before parliament. I would ask my hon. friend to allow this to stand. I think he will find the subject dealt with by the Solicitor General in a Bill we propose to introduce.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext: Might I ask the First Minister if he will permit this Bill to go to a second reading in order that I may give the reasons for introducing it ? It will only take a few minutes.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)

speechtext: Certainly.

The Bill I am introducing consists of only three clauses. The object of the first clause is to altar the form of oath provided in the Election Act to be taken by persons who come in and say they have a right to vote, but whose names are not on the voters' list. It was found in some constituencies in Ontario that persons came in and claimed the right to vote for a reason that was never contemplated by the Act. The Franchise Act passed in 1898 sets forth cleanly the reasons to be assigned toy the voter for asking for a ballot if his name is not on the list, and they are as follows :
(a) The holder of an office, or (b) any person employed in any capacity in the public servico of Canada or in the province, or (c) any person belonging to or engaged in any profession, calling, employment or occupation, or (d) a person belonging to any other class of persons who, although possessed of the qualifications gene-ally required by the provincial law, are by such law declared to be disqualified by reason of their belonging to such class.
Notwithstanding these reasons, some deputy returning officers, by mistake, I assume, permitted voters to assign other reasons than any of those I have read, as came out in the trial of the North Bruce election. One man said the reason he was left off was because he was neglected. Another man swore that the reason he was left off was of a somewhat similar character, because he was absent. Now these reasons were never contemplated by the election law. The intention was to provide for those cases that occur in the province of Nova Scotia where all Dominion officials are left off the provincial list, and, as a matter of course, off the Dominion list. The intention then of the first and third clauses is to provide against the possibility of such a practice by deputy returning officers. Instead of leaving a blank in the oath, I propose that the whole space be filled up by inserting the various reasons provided for by the Franchise Act ; and then when a voter chooses the particular reason which he will swear to, the other three reasons are to be eliminated. In this way il hope the difficulty will be got over. I may say that in drafting the Bill I inadvertently left out the latter clause of the oath, but that can easily be amended in Committee of the Whole.
The other clause of the Bill is intended to prevent errors by voters marking their ballots above the bar over the first name. In the county which I have the honour to represent that mistake occurred. Persons came in and marked their cross above the bar. Illiterate voters are frequently told to vote opposite the first name or the second name. There have been cases of that kind, and voters thinking they were properly marking their ballot by putting the cross over the bar instead of opposite the name, lest their votes. A peculiar case occurred in the election of my hon. friend from

Peel (Mr. Blain), which I will mention to show the far-reaching effect an error may have. The man who printed the ballots was named Dick, I do not know his first name ; his name appeared at the top of the ballot over the bar. Now, our hon., friend who represents the county of Peel is named Richard Blain, and is familiarly known as Dick Blain amongst his friends. Some 25 electors in the county thought they were voting for Dick Blain when they actually put the cross opposite the name of Mr. Dick who printed the ballot. Now, by having no space above the bar the possibility of such a thing would not occur. The proposal is that, in the words of the Bill:
Form P in the schedule I to the said Act is amended so that the broad black line above the first name on the ballot paper shall extend to the upper edge of the ballot paper, and the broad black line below the last name on the ballot paper shall extend to the lower edge of the ballot paper.
I propose that there shall 'be no space outside, either above or (below tbe 'black bar, and this will prevent tbe possibility of a voter marking his ballot outside tbe space which is intended.

I would like to ask the right hon. gentleman whether, in this Bill which he proposes to bring down on behalf of the government, there will be a provision for avoiding what happened in the West Durham election. There, the gentleman who received a majority of the votes, by reason of some technicality raised by the returning officer, is not in his seat here to-day. There ought to he some provision in the law by which summary action would be secured in a case of that kind. There is a provision in the municipal law under which disputes of a similar character are referred at once to a single judge, and within a week you can get a decision. A case might arise where, if there were a dozen returning officers in the country, and they happened to be strongly partisan, and if tbe election proved to be very close, and those dozen returning officers declined to act or raised a technical objection, the government would be in tbe hands of a. party that did not have the majority of the votes of the people. Not only can this serious wrong be done to an individual and to a constituency, but by tbe present defect in the law a great wrong could be done to the whole country ; and I hope when the hon. gentleman is bringing in a Bill he will provide some kind of an appeal to a county judge, who will see that the intention of the people under the circumstances is respected and that their choice is returned to parliament. While I say this, I do not dispute the right of this House now, if it saw fit, to seat Mr. Thornton for West Durham, without any reference to the courts.
I believe it is to the discredit of parliament to-day that we have not righted that wrong,
and that Mr. Thornton is not sitting in the House as the representative of that riding. 1 am much in favour of leaving disputed election cases, as a general rule, to the judges and to the law of the land ; but in this case the law is defective, and parliament would be certainly exercising its just rights, and probably the right hon. gentleman would only be doing his duty if he came down to this House and made a proposal that Mr. Thornton should be allowed to take his seat as member for West Durham.

X wish to add a word to the remarks just made by the hou. member for East York (Mr. Maclean). Mr. Thornton won his seat fairly, so far as any one knows. The right hon. gentleman will remember that when the law was amended only a few years ago, in relation to the deposit of a candidate, the intention was then to avoid the possibility of a returning officer declaring the election void or electing a candidate of his choice. The intention was clear that the receipt which the returning officer gave ihould he a guarantee to the candidate and all concerned that the deposit was perfectly valid. I think that if the remarks, made in the House at that time, are referred to. that will be found to have been tbe motive cause. X am not entering into the discussion here to-night of the question of the voiding of the seat, but I wish to suggest to the right hon. Prime Minister that when the Bill is brought before the House, the point involved in the West Durham election will be placed beyond peradventure. There is another Issue. The matter has not been brought before the House so far as I know during this session. It is in relation to a case which is, I believe, before the courts, and possibly it Is out of order to discuss it here upon its merits, but I am referring to it merely In order that safeguards may be put in the law to prevent a repetition of tbe Nipisslng scandal. Here we find a returning officer hiding on the day of nomination, secreting himself, in order that the legal nomination may not be held, and having what we call an irregular nomination subsequently held. I would like to suggest to the right hon. gentleman that the law be so amended that errors of that kind, intentional or otherwise, should not be committed in future, and that no man should hold a seat in this House under such circumstances as the hon. member now representing Nipissing holds his seat here. Another point is this : We find that men who have been living for years out of the riding, but who chanced to be registered as farmers' sons, or owners, or occupants, are brought in to vote. I will not say one side does it any more than the other ; but the section of the law is not clear as to how long a man may be absent. It applies to lumbermen, labourers and students who are

absent from their homes. I would suggest to the right lion, gentleman that the section should receive his attention. A hired man living in one riding moves to another one ; he gets his washing done at his own home, and so on. I just bring in that one illustration. Where does that man vote ? There are a great many votes lost on each side owing to this, and a great many votes improperly cast owing to the improper construction of the law. I trust the right hon. gentleman will give these suggestions his consideration.

I have no objection to allowing this Bill to go to its second reading, because 1 find most of the provisions which are contained in it are also contained in the Bill to be introduced by tne non. Solicitor General (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick). My hon. friend (Mr. Ingram) will be satisfied to know that the mistake which he wishes to provide against in so far as the marking of the ballot is concerned, is provided for in the Bill which is to be introduced to-morrow. There will be no space above upon which such an error may be repeated as that which occurred in the last election. In regard to the other provisions of the Bill, a provision which enacts that no one shall be permitted to vote whose name is not on the list except those who are specially provided for, I believe, is also contained in the Bill. Therefore, I will allow this Bill to go to its second reading, subject to it being taken up later on, if my hon. friend is not satisfied with the Bill which the government proposes to bring in. In regard to my hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean). I am happy to say that the mistake which took place in West Durham is not to be repeated either. First of all, my hon. friend must allow that there is an improvement. The man who got the minority of votes in West Durham is not in the House. In former times he would have taken his seat in this House. But, the Bill provides. I believe, that if such a mistake as took place in West Durham occurs, it will not avail, because there is a provision in the Bill to be introduced that an accepted cheque will be sufficient deposit instead of money. As to the objection of my hon. friend from North Victoria (Mr. Hughes), I doubt whether we shall be able to meet all the requirements of his fastidious taste. We will try to do our best, but if we do not succeed it will be open for him to offer such amendments as he thinks best when the Bill comes up for consideration in the committee.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext: I would like to ask the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) whether the counterfoil of the government ballot is to be black ?
Yes, the ballot will be black.
I mean the counterfoil attached to the ballot.
I cannot say as to that.

Mr. Speaker, in respect to what has been suggested by some hon. members of this House as to a summary mode of dealing with mistakes made by returning officers, I think the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and the Solicitor General (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) might well keep that suggestion in mind, notwithstanding what the Prime Minister has said. For example, there is a summary way of dealing with questions respecting the proper or improper marking of ballots that is open to a summary proceeding before the county court judge. It has occurred to me, in thinking over the West Durham case, that mistakes by the deputy returning officer or the returning officer, which brought about these very bad results in West Durham, might possibly be dealt with in the courts in some way other than by the cumbrous machinery of an election petition. I believe in having these matters dealt with by the courts. I have no doubt the House could amend the return in the West Durham case, but it did not seem desirable to bring that matter up in the House for the reason that the question had been committed to the courts, and I do not think the House should attempt to deal with it. But, while I say that, I do not think it would require a very great effort to so amend the Controverted Elections Act, that certain matters of that class might be dealt with in a summary way by some tribunal, as the question of proper or improper marking of ballots is now dealt with upon application before a county court judge. I trust that the hon. Solicitor General will take that matter into consideration, and see whether it is possible to make some additional provision in that regard. I would like to point out to the right hon. gentleman that although he amends the law in this respect, that does not obviate the possibility of a returning officer in future making mistakes of a similar character.

Mr. Speaker, that case, I should think, would be a very proper case to. go before the Committee on Privileges and Elections. We have a right here to deal with it, and but for the fact that it was first taken to the courts, I think it would be proper to bring it before the Privileges and Elections Committee, and deal with it in a comparatively summary way.
May I ask the right hon. gentleman (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) will he, under the circumstances and in view of this Bill, bring down a resolution giving Mr. Thornton the seat for West Durham ?

My hon. friend is a little bit of a radical, I am afraid. I

do not know that lie would advise me seriously to take the case out of the courts and bring it into parliament.
Yes, I would.
I do not think I am prepared for that.

I would like to ask the right hon. Prime Minister if he has examined any of the ballot-voting machines. I do not mean the professional ones that have been so aptly managed by hon. gentlemen opposite, but the ordinary voting machines. There are a number before the public, and I am satisfied that they do their work perfectly and accurately.
I have seen a great many of these machines, and I stand by the ballot. I think that with a little attention very few mistakes must take place in future with the form of ballot we have now.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time.

subtopic: WEIGHTS AND MEASURES ACT-SIZE OF FRUIT BASKETS.
WEIGHTS AND MEASURES ACT-SIZE OF FRUIT BASKETS.
speechtext:
SMITH (Wentworth) moved second reading of Bill (No. 10) to amend the Weights and Measures Act.
He said :	I presume it will he expected
that I should briefly give the reasons for the introduction of this Bill. Many hon. members are no doubt aware that up to the present time we have had no standard size for fruit baskets. Many years ago, when fruit-growing first became an important industry, baskets were manufactured that were thought to be most suitable for different kinds of fruit, and custom established these baskets at certain standards. The largest of these is described in the Bill as a 15-quart basket, and it was used for shipping grapes by the ton. That basket still remains about the same size, and as the fruit is sold by the pound there was no inducement for any one to make a different basket. The second largest basket ; the 11-quart basket was originally made a 12-quart basket which was thought to be about the right size to conveniently ship peaches, pears, plumbs, quinces, apricots and tomatoes. It was not very long, however, before some smart 'Aleck ' thought he could make money by reducing the size of the basket to lli quarts, and as it was the same shape as the 12-quart basket, the only difference being a quarter of an inch in the depth, he found that he could sell it for the same price as a 12-quart basket. This went on for a time and then some one invented the 11-quart basket, until at the present time the basket that is called a 12-quart basket in some cases only holds 9 quarts. These baskets are all sold as ' baskets,' and not as holding any par-34
ticular quantity of fruit, but the consumer believes that he is getting a basket holding 32 quarts. It may surprise some to know that the consumers do not know the difference, but experience shows that to be the case, and consequently the producer who ships his fruit in an honest 12-quart basket, or even in an 11-quart basket, is defrauded because the average basket to-day only holds about 10J quarts. At a recent meeting a fruit-grower very happily put it when he said : The fruit producer is placed in a dilemma, because if he ships in an honest 12-quart basket he cheats himself, and if he ships in a 10-quart basket he cheats his customer, so betwixt the two he is sure to sin. In regard to the next size of basket described in the Bill as 6| quarts, there are several sizes used at present containing various quantities between 6 quarts and 74 quarts. This Bill seeks to do away with these various sizes, and to substitute one that practical men believe will fill the purpose of these different sizes. There is at present no standard. The smaller basket is called a 5-pound basket. Some ship in a basket that holds an honest 5 pounds, while others ship in baskets that hold 4 pounds and 3} pounds. As to the fifth size which is the strawberry box, I believe a Bill was introduced in former sessions to regulate this size. The size specified in this Bill is the standard size in a large section of this country. I may say, Mr. Speaker, that the need of this Bill is so great that the Ontario Fruit Growers Association, a body of men representing the best fruit men in the province, passed a resolution last December appointing a committee to draft the details and arrange for the size of baskets they thought best suitable to the trade. That committee met at Grimsby a couple of weeks ago, and in conjunction with subcommittees from various other associations all over the Niagara district, they recommended certain sizes as being suitable, and practically drafted this Bill. Some objected to making a hard and fast rule as to size because there might be times when baskets would be hard to obtain in this country, and would have to be imported from the United States. To meet that difficulty it was proposed that baskets which were different from the sizes mentioned in the Bill Mioukl be stamped in plain letters with the contents of the basket. These are the main features of the Bill. The reasons why the sizes have been adopted will, I presume, be inquired into at a later stage.

subtopic: WEIGHTS AND MEASURES ACT-SIZE OF FRUIT BASKETS.
speechtext:
I do not rise to oppose in any way the principle of this Bill, because I believe that a well-defined standard for fruit baskets is a very desirable thing. But, notwithstanding the fact that the hon. gentleman from Wentworth (Mr. Smith) has a thorough knowledge of the fruit business, and knows more about packing fruit than perhaps all the



members of this House put together ; yet 1 (hire to suggest to him that possibly he has not struck the best mode of determining the size of the berry basket. This matter was very fully discussed last session, and the session before, when I had the opportunity of meeting men who are well acquainted with that line of business. The impression seemed to be then that the better way to define the size of the berry box was by making it so many inches square at the top, so many inches square at the bottom, and so many inches deep, thus fixing the size by inches, and not by measurement in the form of a quart or four-fiftlis of a quart. My reason for thinking that mode of determining the size of the berry basket the better one, is this : A man may go on the market in Montreal to buy a box of berries and desiring to know if he is getting a box of the standard size he has no quart measure or four-fifths of a quart measure with him, but he has a rule in his pocket with which he can determine in three seconds whether the basket is 4J inches square at the top, 4 inches square at the bottom, and 2J inches in depth. If	that is the size, he
knows he has a standard box, and is getting all the berries he pays for; but in the other way it would be very difficult for a man to know whether he was receiving the proper quantity or not. I do not wish to oppose the principle of the Bill, because in the county which I have the honour to represent, a very large quantity of small fruits are grown and shipped to the larger markets of Toronto and Montreal, and my constituents are very much interested in a measure of this kind. I hope the hon. gentleman will not press the Bill too rapidly through the House, so that we may have an opportunity of hearing from persons interested in it; and it may be that at a later stage he will accept the suggestion as to the mode of defining the standard box instead of the one he proposes in the Bill.

subtopic: WEIGHTS AND MEASURES ACT-SIZE OF FRUIT BASKETS.
speechtext: I do not rise to oppose the Bill, because I do not profess to be sufficiently familiar with the details of the business to take exception to many portions of it. I simply rise to ask that the House be very cautious in accepting this measure, on this ground, that while it may be satisfactory to the gentlemen forming the Fruit Growers' Association of Ontario, dealing as they do with a definite trade well understood by them, there is much danger that a measure covering in its operations the whole Dominion of Canada, if passed by this House, might work great hardships on many people in various portions of the country. I very much fear that this Bill, if passed in its present form, would be found oppressive and unsatisfactory in many portions of the maritime provinces; and if the measure ever reaches the committee stage, I will move that until fur-

speechtext: ther information can be gained, the province of Nova Scotia be exempted from its operation. Another thing: as the whole subject of weights and measures applicable to berries and fruits of all kinds as well as other things, is under the control of the Department of Inland Revenue, I would ask my hon. friend who introduced the Bill if it has ever been referred either directly or indirectly to that department to be enquired into and reported upon. It seems to me that in regard to a measure dealing with interests which are large in some places and small in other places, but in every place important, a department of the government charged with making inquiries as to the effect of new legislation of this kind should have an opportunity of examining the Bill and reporting upon it through the experts of that department. In the county which I have the honour to represent which exports annually from $30,000 to $50,000 worth of blueberries, and in which a large part of the population at a certain season of the year is interested in the picking, packing, transporting and selling of those berries, none of the dimensions given here would apply, but the provisions of the Bill would operate with peculiar hardship. Assuming that other portions of the country may have other difficulties of a cognate character, I merely rise to ask the House to be cautious in accepting a measure which, in one portion at any rate, is of a very drastic character, because it makes any violation of the law a criminal offence. ' I would suggest that my hon. friend, if he takes the second reading to-night, allow the Bill to stand for some time before moving it in committee, in order that gentlemen may have further opportunity of looking into it.

speechtext: The suggestions of the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) seem at first sight to be very good, and in many respects I think they are ; but with the baskets made as at present, they would not be practicable, because he gives the square measure top and bottom^ whereas the baskets are usually round.

The baskets for either peaches or grapes are round at the ends. Therefore, a square measure would not do. But for that, I would say that the suggestion was a very good one.

My constituents are largely interested in the milk trade around Toronto, and they have long asked this parliament to give them a standard milk can. There are a lot of these questions coming up constantly, and

I would have liked to see the Minister of Inland Revenue (Hon. Mr. Bernier) here tonight to give his views on this Bill. When it comes up again, I hope he will be here. If parliament deals with a matter of this kind, it must deal with it in a drastic way. It will have to make a lot of standards for almost every trade-an apple barrel, a flour barrel, and many other things; or we shall have to leave everything to the standard of weights and measures recognized in this country. Perhaps on the whole, that would be the best thing to do. Otherwise we shall have to provide a standard for every product raised in the country.

speechtext: I am sorry the Minister of Agriculture (Hon. Mr. Fisher) is not in his seat this evening, as the duty of dealing with this Bill devolves upon me, and I must confess my utter incompetence. However, I am not very much ashamed of that, in view of the differences which exist even among members who are familiar with the subject. We have a difference as to whether the baskets used to-day are square or round. With such a difference on a question of fact, there must necessarily be differences of opinion on the measure; and I am sure that my hon. friend who has brought in the Bill will be satisfied if we take the second reading to-night, and take the committee stage at a future sitting.

speechtext: Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time.

Mr. JAMES CLANCY (Bothwell) moved second reading of Bill (No. 15) further to amend the Dominion Elections Act, 1900.
He said : I move the second reading of this Bill on the understanding that was come to at the suggestion of the right hon. First Minister some days ago, namely, that it be allowed to pass its second reading, and that discussion takes place upon it when the whole subject matter comes up.
I have no objection; but, perhaps, my hon. friend would give us the reasons which led to the introduction of the Bill.

I stated the reasons briefly a few days ago when I introduced it. The purpose of the Bill is to prevent the worst form of intimidation, namely, persons telling voters that the mode of voting is not secret, thus placing the voters at the mercy of those who may state on the one side that the ballot is a secret one, or of others who may state that it is not. Under such circumstances, it is natural that the voter will be improperly influenced. It 34*
seems to me that there is no more insidious form of intimidation than for persons to make statements of that kind. The right hon. gentleman will see himself that it utterly destroys the secrecy of the ballot. That is shortly the object of the Bill, and I trust the right hon. gentleman will allow it to take this stage, with the undertsand-ing that it will be discussed when the whole subject-matter is taken up.

Mr. JABEL ROBINSON (West Elgin) moved the second reading of Bill (No. 16) respecting drainage.
He said ; The object of this Bill is to give to the farmers the same privileges that are enjoyed by the railway companies. Since the country has become cleared up, the farmers are beginning to under drain their land, as it is impossible to successfully cultivate land unless the surplus water is taken out. In many cases where railways have been built, ditches have to be carried beneath the railways, and the railways are not amenable to the same laws as the farmers. This Bill will make the railway companies contribute towards the cost of those ditches the same as the farmers. The amendment to the Railway Act of last year reads as follows :
Whenever proceedings for the drainage of lands have been taken by any landowner under the provisions of an Act of the legislature of any province in that behalf, and it appears to the Railway Committee that an outlet for such drainage works is required over, across or under the lands of the company, the Railway Committee may, upon the application of the landowner or engineer in charge of the works, or of the clerk of the municipality and on due notice to and hearing the parties, order the company to construct and provide upon its lands all necessary means of drainage, as in such order specified upon the landowner first complying with such terms as to payment as to the whole or so much of the cost of construction and maintenance of the said drainage work as the Railway Committee in such order provides.
This is the clause that stings the farmers all through Ontario. In many cases it would cost the farmer more money to apply to tha.t Railway Committee and make the payments here required than the land would be worth. We require, consequently, that the railway companies should come under the same law as the farmer. All we have to do to accomplish this is to put in these few words into the Railway Act and take clause 14a out of it. I hope the farmers in this House will appreciate this measure and thoroughly examine it, and if they are satisfied no doubt the other hon. members will be satisfied also. If this Bill is allowed to go to committee, the farmers thoroughly understand it and will be able to convince that committee of its necessity. The farmers of this country have expressed themselves in stronger language against the Min-

ister of Railways for having put that clause in last session than for all the other sins this government committed last summer.
I trust that this matter will he taken up and handled in the proper spirit.

I am very much afraid, if the hon. gentleman's view of the result of my action in this matter last session be correct, that in endeavouring to have this legislation put into the shape in which I think it ought, to be, in order to fully safeguard the public interest, I will be discharging a very thankless duty. This is happily a question which does not partake of a political character, and which we can therefore deal with solely on its merits and come to the wisest conclusion at which our judgments will enable us to arrive, without being hampered in the slightest by political considerations. I am not going to suggest that this Bill should not pass through its second reading, but I would ask the hon. gentleman to have it referred to the Select Standing Committee on Railways and Canals so that it may undergo discussion in that committee.
There is more in the matter, I can assure the hon. gentleman, than he and his friends and the people who are calling for this legislation imagine, a great deal more. It involves the complete and total surrender by this parliament to the local authorities which are constituted under provincial drainage Acts of the means to be taken for the protection of life and property against the possibility of casualty resulting from carelessness in the way in which roadbeds of railways may be affected by this procedure. The duty is cast upon us as a parliament of seeing that the railways of the country are operated safely, that nothing that is necessary for the protection of those who use the railways-both, as I said, as to their lives and as to their property-shall be overlooked. And it will be a matter for the Railway Committee, and, if necessary, later, for this House to see whether or not that proper and necessary protection can be secured if this Bill becomes law. I take that to be a larger and more important consideration than the one which the hon. gentleman would wish to see provided for. I do not for a moment dissent from the view that this is a very important matter for people residing in many sections of the country. I can well conceive that it would be a great advantage to them if some means could be adopted, consistent with the proper protection of life and property, which would enable them to drain their property under more favourable conditions than, it appears, by law, they are now able to do. I grant the importance of the matter which the hon. gentleman has in view ; but we must not overlook the importance of the other considerations. It is the duty of parliament to weigh both and to examine both. We will Mr. ROBINSON (West Elgin).
do that, I trust and believe, according to our very best judgment and ability when the matter comes to be considered by the Railway Committee, to which I would suggest that the Bill be referred. Let me say one word with regard to the legislation of last session. It is open under that legislation for any landowner to give notice to the Railway Committee that he has utilized the machinery which he has at his hand at home, and the Railway Committee, being then set in motion, can work the problem out.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS (Hon. A. G. Blair).

speechtext: I would ask the hon. gentleman whether the legislation of last session has resulted in any cases coming before the Railway Committee of the Privy Council ?

I was just going to say that that has been done in one or two cases. I know of one ease, and I am under the impression that there was another, but cannot speak with confidence as to that. The parties did not require to send a delegation to Ottawa. They were told, when the Bill was before the House last session, that a simple letter would answer all purposes. A letter was written informing my department that a case had arisen which was within the contemplation of the Act of last year. We immediately sent an engineer for the purpose, and he met the parties, and they met the railway people. There was no further complaint about it, and I understood that an understanding satisfactory to all had been reached without any serious expense to the party. That is as far as I can speak with confidence at this moment. I believe that could be worked out ; 1 know of no reason why it could not be done. I think it is not possible for any one to say that they have endeavoured to utilize the procedure of last year and have failed. I am confident that that has not occurred, for if it had occurred, I am sure I should have known of it. I would urge that we do not deal with this matter too hastily, because we cannot conceive what the consequences might be if such a change as is proposed becomes the law of the land. There is one matter the hon. gentleman complains of which is not so easy of adjustment, and that is with regard to the expense that must be incurred when these works are required to be carried on, and the distribution which may be made by the officers of the department or by agreement between the parties as to the portion which each should bear of the cost. I can well believe that it would be somewhat burdensome, perhaps it might be found to be beyond the means of the applicants to comply with the requirements of the Act. But that is no ground of objection to the law. We can well imagine that conditions will arise that cannot possibly be remedied. But, if you are

going to insure fair treatment to all parties in such controversies, when such a question arises you must impose obligations upou each, and if the obligations appear to be heavier upon one than the other, if one of the parties is less able to bear what he justly ought to bear than the other party, that is no ground for criticism of the haw. We cannot prevent these conditions from existing ; we must take things as they are. And, therefore, I can see that it might be almost impossible to remedy the complaint which the hon. gentleman has dwelt upon with respect to the probable cost which may be imposed upon the landowner who would secure the right of making a drain or constructing works through or under the road-bed of a railway. 1 am content. as I said, that every opportunity should be afforded the hon. gentleman, and those who think with him, to thresh the question out again before the Railway Committee. Or, after it reaches there, should it be deemed wise to take that course, I would favour it being referred to a sub-committee for. perhaps, a closer and more thorough inquiry than would be possible before the whole committee.
Motion agreed to ; Bill read the second time, and referred to the Select Standing Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lilies.
